about.title: About
about.p1: {name} shows how Spain has changed in recent years using official statistics, and translates the proposals in party programmes into numbers so that anyone can check them against the data.
about.p2: Every figure, chart and assessment links to its source: the publisher, the table, the date it was downloaded and the calculation. The downloaded files are kept in the public repository.

funding.title: Funding and independence
funding.body: This project receives no funding, advertising or endorsement from any political party, and does not accept any.

principles.title: Principles
principles.sameRubric: The same method applies to every party, in the same batch. The method was written down before it was applied to any party.
principles.blind: Proposals are assessed without the party name or logo; the party is attached afterwards.
principles.noCausal: The data show what changed, not who caused it. Context markers are dated facts only.
principles.traceable: Any number can be traced to the downloaded file it came from.
principles.corrections: Corrections are listed publicly with the date, what changed and why.

open.title: Open source

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.intro: How the data are collected and processed, how parties and proposals are selected, and how proposals are assessed.

data.title: Data
data.p1: Data come from official publishers: INE, Eurostat, Banco de España, the Tax Agency (AEAT), Seguridad Social and ministries. Where a publisher offers an API, it is used; otherwise the published file is downloaded.
data.p2: Every downloaded file is stored unchanged in the public repository with its SHA-256 hash, address and download date. Values are then extracted by code that reads only those stored files, so the same files always give the same numbers.
data.p3: Topic pages show {year} to the latest figure available. The CSV for each indicator contains the full series. Values are shown as published; no seasonal adjustment or other modelling is added unless the indicator says so.
data.p4: Each card's sentence compares the latest figure with the same quarter or month of the first year shown, so seasonal series are compared like with like. Each topic's headline is the first indicator listed for that topic in the project brief.
data.p5: A weekly automated job downloads the sources again and opens a review request with the changes. Nothing is published without a person approving it.
data.events: Charts mark a few dated events. They are facts with a date and a source, not explanations of the data.
data.p6: Forecasts and projections are those published by the IMF, the European Commission, AIReF and the EU Ageing Report; we make none of our own. They are drawn as dashed lines and marked f, each with its publication date and its own definition.

indicators.title: Indicators
indicators.intro: Every published indicator with its source, calculation and download. Raw-file links point to the exact bytes used.
indicators.notOnDashboard: used in calculations, not shown on topic pages

parties.title: Parties and proposals
parties.coalitions: Coalitions are listed under the name voters saw on the ballot, using the programme filed for that election. Later changes in parliamentary groups do not change the list.
parties.programs: Each programme is archived in the repository with its SHA-256 hash, original address, download date and a Wayback Machine copy, so quotes remain checkable if the original disappears.
parties.extraction: Proposals are split out of the programme with the help of a language model, offline. A person reviews every proposal before publication (draft → reviewed → published). No text is generated when a page is visited.
parties.selection: About 10–15 proposals per party, preferring those the party itself highlights in summaries or lists of main commitments, so the selection is not editorial.

assessment.title: Assessment method

status.proposed: proposed, not yet frozen; no assessment has been made with it
status.frozen: frozen and applied to all parties

assessment.scope: Proposals with a cost, a revenue effect or a numerical target get an assessment card with these parts:

fields.baseline: Baseline: the current value and recent trend, with source.
fields.required: Required change: per year, in absolute terms and in percent, or the cost in euros and as a share of GDP.
fields.benchmark: Historical benchmark: the largest comparable change in Spain since 2000, and the EU-27 range where useful.
fields.funding: Funding identified: yes, partial, no or not applicable, based only on what the programme says.
fields.estimates: Independent estimates (AIReF, Banco de España, Fedea, OECD, academic work), or a statement that none were found.
fields.calculation: The formula and inputs, stored so the calculation can be re-run from the repository.
fields.confidence: Confidence: high, medium or low, depending on how directly the data measure what the proposal targets.

bands.consistent: Consistent with recent data: the required change is no larger than the largest change observed in Spain over a comparable period since 2000.
bands.ambitious: Ambitious: larger than Spain's largest observed change, but within the largest observed in an EU-27 country.
bands.unprecedented: Beyond any observed precedent: larger than both.
bands.not_assessable: Not assessable: rule changes and statements of intent without a number. They are listed but not scored.
bands.costNotCovered: Cost not covered: a proposal costing more than {threshold} of GDP a year with no funding identified. Shown alongside the band, not instead of it.

assessment.noScore: There is no overall party score. Each party page shows how many proposals fall in each band, by topic, and the yearly cost of costed proposals next to the funding the party identified.
assessment.blind: Proposals are assessed without the party name or logo; the party is attached after scoring.

neutrality.title: Neutrality
neutrality.sameRubric: One rubric for all parties. Changes create a new version that is re-applied to every party at once.
neutrality.noCausal: No claims that a government caused or deserves credit for any change.
neutrality.language: Neutral wording only: bands and measured statements, no adjectives about parties or proposals.
neutrality.colours: Party colours appear only on the party chip, never in charts or assessments.
neutrality.readings: Green and red marks follow one fixed rule per indicator (see Favourable and unfavourable marks) and never refer to a party or a government.
neutrality.headline: Parties are ordered by seats at the last general election, then alphabetically.
neutrality.translations: Spanish is the source language. Translations of methodology and results go through the same review status as the content.
neutrality.corrections: All corrections are listed on the corrections page.

distributions.title: Distributions: average, median, most common, P90, P99
distributions.p1: The average (mean) is the total divided by the number of people. The median (P50) is the amount that splits the group in half. The most common amount is the range where people are most concentrated. P90 is the amount above which the top 10% are; P99, the top 1%. When an average is far above the median, a minority with large amounts pulls it up.
distributions.p2: Where a source publishes percentiles (INE, Eurostat, Banco de España), they are used as published. Where it only publishes how many people fall in each amount bracket (Tax Agency, Seguridad Social), percentiles are estimated (marked ≈): inside a bracket whose total amount is published, amounts follow a power law fitted so the bracket's average matches the published one; inside a bracket without amounts, people are assumed evenly spread; in the open top bracket, a Pareto tail is fitted from its average. If that is not possible, only “more than” the bracket's lower bound is given.
distributions.p3: The most common amount is the densest range of equal width when brackets are narrow, the densest published bracket when they are medium, and it is not shown when brackets are too wide to tell.
distributions.p4: Populations differ and are not directly comparable: tax returns (a joint return counts once), people, pensions, or households; gross or net amounts; per year, per month, or a stock of wealth. Each table and card says which.
distributions.p5: When a proposal targets a group defined by an amount (for example “incomes above €100,000”), its assessment card states the share and number of people above that amount in the matching distribution, with the same method.

readings.title: Favourable and unfavourable marks
readings.p1: Some cards mark the latest change as favourable (green tick), unfavourable (red triangle) or in line (grey equals sign). Each indicator has one fixed rule, listed below. The rules are the same for every period and every government, and a mark says nothing about who caused a change.
readings.p2: Prices and incomes are compared with the Consumer Price Index (CPI) over the same span: real change = (1 + nominal change) / (1 + CPI change) − 1. For prices (housing, rents), rising less than the CPI is favourable, because they become cheaper relative to other goods; for incomes (wages, pensions), rising more than the CPI is favourable, because purchasing power grows. Growth rates are compared with the CPI annual rate for the same period.
readings.p3: Quarters and years use the average of INE's monthly index; a year still in progress uses the months published so far, against the same months a year earlier, and says so. A difference smaller than {pp}, or {pct} in real terms, counts as in line.
readings.p4: Real GDP growth is already net of price changes, so it is not compared with the CPI: positive growth is marked favourable.
readings.p5: Other indicators are compared with their value a year earlier and with the first year shown. Changes smaller than 0.1 pp (0.5 pp for shares of GDP, which are large and often revised) or 0.1% count as no change. The deficit and debt are compared both with the EU reference values and with their own change.
readings.p6: Inflation is compared with the ECB's 2% target (within ±0.5 pp is favourable); the deficit and debt with the EU reference values of 3% and 60% of GDP.
readings.p7: Spending by function, revenue, demography and migration are not rated: no direction is favourable for everyone. Nor are sexual offences and online fraud known to the police, because changes in reporting and in the Criminal Code move them as much as how often they happen, nor the unadjusted pay gap, which also changes when who works, and in what, changes (not only when pay for the same work changes). Their cards show only which way they moved, with a grey arrow.
readings.p8: On the home page, each topic shows the change in its headline indicator and the count of all marks on the topic page, from the first year shown (an indicator repeated at another frequency is counted once). The card's top edge is split green, grey and red in the same proportions.

spending.title: Where each €100 goes ({year})
spending.intro: All levels of government spent {total} and collected {taxes} in taxes and social contributions.
spending.financingTitle: How each €100 of spending was paid for
spending.financingNote: Other revenue includes sales of goods and services, property income and transfers. Borrowing is the deficit, which adds to public debt.
spending.perTaxTitle: Per €100 collected in taxes and social contributions
spending.perTaxNote: Above €100 means spending exceeded taxes and contributions; the rest came from other revenue and borrowing.
spending.noteCofog: Functional classification COFOG (Eurostat), all levels of government. Old age is mostly pensions; it sits inside social protection. Public debt transactions are mostly interest.
spending.noteDefence: Defence here follows COFOG and is lower than NATO's figure for Spain, which also counts military pensions, the Guardia Civil's military duties and defence spending by other ministries.
spending.noteOtherSocial: Other social protection covers sickness, disability, survivors, family, unemployment, housing benefits and social exclusion.

jobs.title: Jobs gained or lost by occupation ({start} to {end})
jobs.summary: Employment changed by {total}: {high} ({highShare}) as managers, professionals and technicians; {medium} ({mediumShare}) in middle-skill occupations; {elementary} ({elementaryShare}) in elementary occupations.
jobs.chartTitle: Change in people employed, by occupation (CNO-11 major group)
jobs.noteSkill: Skill levels follow ISCO-08: groups 1–3 need the highest skill levels (usually higher education), 4–8 intermediate skills, 9 elementary tasks. The occupation is the job held, not the person's qualification.
jobs.noteSeason: Same quarter in both years, to avoid seasonal differences. EPA survey estimates.

barCard.changeNote: Change in each group's or item's price index over the same month; not each household's spending, which depends on what it buys. ECOICOP ver. 2 groups of INE's CPI.

pensionsExplainer.title: How pensions are financed
pensionsExplainer.intro: Spain's public pensions are pay-as-you-go: the contributions paid by today's workers and employers fund today's pensions, and the State covers the difference. There are no individual pension accounts. These panels use the official series on this page.
pensionsExplainer.whoText: {affiliates} people pay contributions (Social Security affiliates) and {pensions} contributory pensions are paid: {ratio} affiliates per pension.
pensionsExplainer.typesTitle: What kinds of pensions are paid
pensionsExplainer.typesText: Retirement pensions are {share} of contributory pensions; the rest are widowhood, permanent disability, orphanhood and family pensions.
pensionsExplainer.balanceText: In a pay-as-you-go system, contributions equal pensions when the contribution rate equals the average pension as a share of the average wage, divided by the number of contributors per pension. Move the two levers to see the rate that would balance the system.
pensionsExplainer.calcReplacement: Average pension as % of average wage
pensionsExplainer.defaults: Today's values: average contributory pension {pension} a month × 14 ({pensionPeriod}); INE average gross annual wage {wage} ({wagePeriod}).
pensionsExplainer.simplification: Simplified identity: it leaves out the maximum contribution base, the lower bases of the self-employed, the share of contributions that pays sick and birth leave, and non-contributory pensions. It shows the order of magnitude, not the actual deficit.
pensionsExplainer.simulator: To estimate a personal pension with the legal rules, use the Seguridad Social simulator:
pensionsExplainer.ratesSplit: Who pays and what it funds

pensionsOutlook.title: Who pays and who receives? Today and in 4, 10 and 20 years
pensionsOutlook.intro: Official projections if laws and current trends do not change: the EU 2024 Ageing Report for contributors, pensioners, spending and contributions, and INE for the population by age. They are not our own forecasts. Move the slider to see each year.
pensionsOutlook.today: Observed ({period}, Seguridad Social): {affiliates} affiliates and {pensions} contributory pensions ({pensioners} pensioners), that is {ratio} affiliates per pension.
pensionsOutlook.pyramidTitle: Population by age and sex, 1 January {year}
pensionsOutlook.workingPerOlder: people aged 16–66 per person aged 67 or over
pensionsOutlook.pyramidAlt: Population pyramid on 1 January {year}: {young} aged 0–15, {working} aged 16–66 and {older} aged 67 or over.
pensionsOutlook.noteProjection: The projections assume no change to the laws in force when they were prepared (the 2024 Ageing Report includes reforms up to 2023) and that fertility, mortality and migration trends continue. They are scenarios, not predictions.
pensionsOutlook.noteDefinitions: The Ageing Report counts people who contribute and people who receive pensions in all public schemes (including civil servants' Clases Pasivas), so its figures differ from Seguridad Social's affiliates and pensions.
pensionsOutlook.noteAges: 67 is the ordinary retirement age from 2027 and 16 the minimum working age. Not everyone aged 16–66 works, and not everyone aged 67 or over receives a pension.

genderPayGap.title: Gender pay gap: in the same job?
genderPayGap.intro: There are several ways to measure it and they answer different questions. No official statistic compares two people in the same post at the same employer; these are the official measures, from the most comparable to the least.
genderPayGap.summary: With the same measured characteristics, women earn {adjusted} less per hour ({adjustedYear}). In the same occupation group and working full time, they earn between {min} and {max} of what men earn ({groupYear}). Unadjusted, the average difference is {raw} ({rawYear}).
genderPayGap.step1: Same measured characteristics (the closest to "the same job")
genderPayGap.step1Text: Eurostat compares women and men with the same occupation, sector, enterprise size and type, contract, working time, experience, education, age and region, and estimates the part of the difference those characteristics do not explain. That part does not by itself prove discrimination, because it includes factors the survey does not measure (the exact post, the specific employer, schedules, negotiation), but it does not rule it out either. In Spain it is larger than the unadjusted difference.
genderPayGap.step2: Same occupation group, full time, per hour ({year})
genderPayGap.step2Text: Full-time women's hourly pay as a % of full-time men's in the same major occupation group (100 = equal). It removes the effect of part-time work and compares similar occupations, though each group includes different jobs.
genderPayGap.step3: Unadjusted: all women compared with all men
genderPayGap.step3Text: This is the EU's official indicator. It does not compare the same job: it measures the average difference, which also reflects that more women work part time or in lower-paid occupations and sectors. It answers a different question (how much each earns on average), not whether the same job is paid differently. That is why it has no green or red mark.
